name: Ancestral lifestyle (Liver King)

lead: The ancestral lifestyle is a regimen popularized from 2021 by American influencer Brian Johnson, known as Liver King. Wikipedia says it rests on nine "ancestral tenets", including rejecting modern conveniences and intense exercise, and it is best known for eating large amounts of raw organ meat, especially liver.[1]

The appearance goal is a lean, heavily muscled, primal physique, which followers read as proof of the method. Johnson denied using steroids until leaked emails in late 2022 reportedly showed spending of over $11,000 a month on performance-enhancing drugs; he then apologized and said he took about 120 mg of testosterone weekly.[1]

paras: Followers describe a mix of meat-heavy eating with organs, hard strength and conditioning work, cold exposure and sleep and outdoor routines framed as ancestral. Supplements sold by Johnson and his wife since 2015 form part of the brand.[1] Specific tenet lists and routines are published by the influencer himself.

Medical professionals cited by Wikipedia criticized the raw-organ approach as potentially dangerous misinformation, noting the heavy-meat diet is high in saturated fat, which is linked to heart disease, high cholesterol and digestive problems.[1] Critics also argue that his physique was largely drug-assisted, which could mislead followers about natural results.[1]

angle.text: Followers adopt the regimen to build muscle and look primal and athletic. The influencer's later admission of steroid use has changed how the outcome is attributed.

lead: The ancestral lifestyle is the regimen promoted since 2020 by Brian Michael Johnson, an American influencer who goes by Liver King. It combines raw and organ-heavy eating, hard strength and conditioning work, and a set of nine "ancestral tenets" that encourage avoiding modern conveniences.[1] Followers adopt it to build a big, lean, primal-looking physique like the one Johnson shows in his videos.

Johnson was born on 2 March 1978 at Naval Station Roosevelt Roads in Ceiba, Puerto Rico, grew up in Texas, and earned a biochemistry degree at Texas Tech University before working in pharmaceutical sales and later holding a stake in his wife Barbara's dental practice.[1] He and Barbara have sold fitness supplements online since 2015, and he co-owns the organ-supplement company Heart & Soil with psychiatrist and carnivore-diet influencer Paul Saladino.[1][2] His videos of eating raw liver and testicles, training in a primitive-styled setting and shouting his "ancestral" message made him one of the most recognisable fitness personalities of 2021.[1]

The topic is best known for a 2022 controversy. After years of presenting his physique as the product of diet and lifestyle, leaked emails reportedly showed he spent more than $11,000 a month on performance-enhancing drugs; Johnson apologised in a video and said he took about 120 mg of testosterone weekly.[1] A 2025 Netflix documentary, Untold: The Liver King, revisited the story.[1] The episode is now widely used in online fitness and looksmaxxing discussion as a reference point for how much of an influencer physique comes from pharmacology versus lifestyle.

paras: The lifestyle is presented as modelled on how ancestral humans ate, moved and lived. Wikipedia describes its core as a raw, meat-and-organ-heavy diet, taxing exercise routines and shunning modern conveniences, organised under nine tenets published by Johnson himself.[1] In his videos the aesthetic is deliberately primal: outdoor training, heavy lifting and conditioning, and a diet centred on liver and other organs.[1]

For people who follow it, the appearance payoff is the physique on display. The chain they describe runs from a nutrient-dense animal-food diet and hard training to more muscle and less body fat.[1] Raw organ eating is also part of the broader nose-to-tail and offal revival; Wikipedia's article on offal notes that consumption has risen in places partly because of fitness influencers.[3]

Johnson has said he was an undersized child who was bullied and had a speech impediment, an account Wikipedia reports as his own claim.[1] His father, an Air Force member, died when he was an infant and his mother raised him and his brother.[1] He married Barbara in 2004, and the couple have two children.[1]

Johnson became active as an influencer in 2020 and went viral in 2021.[1] At the time of the Wikipedia article's latest update he had roughly 6.1 million TikTok followers and 1.22 million YouTube subscribers.[1] His supplement business, begun in 2015, supplied the commercial side of the persona.[1]

sections.h: Heart & Soil and the animal-based scene
paras: Heart & Soil, based in Austin, Texas, sells encapsulated organ-meat supplements and is co-owned by Johnson and Paul Saladino.[1][2] Saladino, born in 1977, holds an MD from the University of Arizona (2015) and completed a psychiatry residency at the University of Washington in 2019; he wrote The Carnivore Code (2020) and later moved from a strict meat-only diet to what he calls an animal-based diet that includes fruit and honey.[2]

The carnivore diet, a meat-and-animal-products eating pattern, has older precedents in the work of nineteenth-century figures such as Arnaldo Cantani and James H. Salisbury, and was popularised on social media from about 2018 by figures such as Shawn Baker, Jordan Peterson and Mikhaila Peterson.[4] Wikipedia lists the animal-based diet, which adds fruit, honey and raw dairy, as a variant that Saladino brought to wide attention in 2024.[4] The Liver King sat at the most visual end of this scene, where the pitch is strength, testosterone and a lean physique.

Johnson repeatedly said his physique was natural and the result of the ancestral lifestyle.[1] In late 2022 private emails leaked, reportedly showing spending of over $11,000 a month on drugs; Wikipedia reports about 16 vials monthly of five steroids and one synthetic protein hormone.[1] Johnson responded with a YouTube apology for misleading viewers about his "pharmacological intervention", acknowledged about 120 mg of testosterone per week, and said there is a "time and place" for such interventions.[1]

Followers filed a lawsuit alleging deception and seeking $25 million; it was later discontinued.[1] Critics argued the episode showed that an influencer's physique can mislead audiences about what a lifestyle alone produces, while Johnson's supporters point to his admission and his continued public presence.[1]

Untold: The Liver King (2025) was directed by Joe Perlman, who said he was interested in what Johnson would do to keep his following.[1] Time's Charlotte Lytton found it not especially critical and doubted Johnson's sincerity, while The Guardian's Rhik Samadder called it witty and often at Johnson's expense.[1] In the film, and in a May 2025 interview, Johnson denounced the carnivore diet and his promotion of it, saying he was wrong.[1]

On 24 June 2025 Austin police arrested Johnson on a Class B misdemeanor charge of terroristic threat, saying he had repeatedly threatened podcaster Joe Rogan on Instagram and travelled to Austin. He was released on $20,000 bail with conditions including no contact with Rogan and a mental health evaluation.[1]

Medical professionals cited by Wikipedia criticised the raw-organ approach as potentially dangerous misinformation and noted that a meat-heavy diet is high in saturated fat, which is associated with heart disease, high cholesterol and digestive problems.[1] Of the carnivore diet more broadly, nutrition scientists and bodies such as the British Dietetic Association and Dietitians Australia classify it as a fad diet and point to raised LDL cholesterol, low fibre, possible nutrient gaps and links between high red-meat intake and colorectal cancer and gout.[4] Saladino's critics, including science communicator Joe Schwarcz, say he overstates risks of plant foods; Saladino himself later reported side effects on a strict carnivore diet, including poor sleep and palpitations.[2]

On looksmax.org the Liver King is mostly discussed through height and frame comparisons; one thread contrasts his build with that of a taller streamer and uses it as an example of a short but muscular influencer.[5] He is also cited in debates about natural versus enhanced physiques.
No studies found on the Liver King regimen as a whole.
